newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Ex-Albanian general takes charge in rebel town.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Albanian general takes charge in rebel town.

text.p: Retired Albanian general Agim Gozhita took charge of this rebel-held southern town on Sunday, ordering teenagers to surrender their weapons and vowing to punish looters.
Gozhita was elected president of a 15-member rebel council in Gjirokaster, 30 kms (20 miles) from the Greek border, just a day after government troops fled in disarray.
While his election took place at the town hall, hundreds of people kept up the looting of a major army base at Gjirokaster and of state food warehouses in the area.
An old woman at the barracks loaded a donkey with blankets and uniforms. Local housewives descended on food warehouses like vultures. Many shops in Gjirokaster had windows smashed and were ransacked.
One person was killed and three were wounded during a night of wild celebrations after rebels seized the town on Saturday. The customs office in the town's centre was burned on Sunday.
The dead and wounded were victims of accidents after rebels and residents pillaged thousands of weapons from depots at the army base, just north of the town.

"There will be no more shootings. Children under 18 should not carry weapons. Shops will open and those caught stealing will be punished," Gozhita told a crowd of 1,500 people in the main square after his election.

He condemned the burning of the customs office and said that state property should be protected. He also said that about 120 soldiers chased off on Saturday should come down from hiding in the nearby mountains.
Local officials said Gozhita, about 40, had been forced out of the army during reforms by President Sali Berisha 18 months ago.

They said Gozhita was from Gjirokaster and had commanded the local army base before he was forced to quit the military. The week-old insurrection in the region has become a personal contest between the rebels and Berisha.
Rebels accuse Berisha of standing by while thousands of Albanians lost their savings in fraudulent investment schemes which collapsed in January. They want him to quit.
Local residents pulled up at the Gjirokaster base throughout the night, collected hundreds of weapons and drove off. Jubliant residents fired wildly into the air.
Gjirokaster, a mountain town of 22,000 people, fell to rebel forces after a failed attempt by Berisha to send in a 120-strong commando unit by helicopters.
Its capture gives rebels a firm grip on the southwest corner of the tiny Balkan country of 3.4 million people, and makes any effort by the military to reconquer the region more difficult.
Rebels now hold the Adriatic coast from Vlore to Sarande -- close to the Greek border and island of Corfu -- and an inland swath of territory from Gjirokaster to Tepelene.
Berisha's offer of amnesty in exchange for surrendering arms by Sunday morning fell on deaf ears throughout the region.
"We will not surrender our weapons unless Berisha resigns," Gozhita told the rally.
With the fall of Gjirokaster, and another big base about 20 kms (12 miles) to the north in Tepelene, the rebels have an increasingly powerful arsenal.
At least 20 rebel tanks roam the region from Sarande to Gjirokaster, and the arsenal at Tepelene yielded at least two dozen heavy artillery pieces.

Retired army officers who were purged by Berisha have taken charge in numerous towns and villages. But at bases like Bajkaji, in the hills above Sarande, Major Ilir Kermezi and his tank unit switched sides en masse last week.
Defensive positions have been set up throughout the region. Big artillery pieces overlook the Tepelene town square. Rebel roadblocks have sprung up everywhere.
The mood is defiant and few of the ex-army officers believe that Berisha can muster a credible military force to take on the southern region.
"Berisha gives deadlines that he cannot inforce," said Ilir, another ex-army officer near Gjiorkaster.
